name: Monocyte
summary: The largest white blood cell, with a big kidney- or horseshoe-shaped nucleus. Monocytes circulate for one to several days, then leave the blood, especially where tissue is inflamed, and turn into macrophages or dendritic-like cells. Most rush to infections; a smaller subset crawls along the inside of blood vessels, checking their lining.
functions: Leaves the blood into infected or injured tissue, arriving after the first neutrophils. Classical monocytes follow the chemokine CCL2 through their receptor CCR2, which they also need to leave the bone marrow.
Turns into a macrophage once in tissue, driven by M-CSF and local signals. In inflamed tissue it can instead become a dendritic-like cell that takes up antigen and shows it to T cells.
Engulfs microbes and dead cells and releases inflammatory cytokines such as TNF, IL-1β and IL-6, even before it changes into a macrophage.
Patrolling (non-classical) monocytes crawl along the inside of blood vessels, clearing damaged lining cells and calling in neutrophils when they find trouble. This was shown mainly in mice.

Humans have three blood subsets: classical (high CD14, no CD16; about 85-90%), intermediate, and non-classical (high CD16). Mice have two, Ly6C-high and Ly6C-low, which match the classical and non-classical types; the intermediate subset has no clear mouse counterpart.

Revised view: monocytes were long thought to be the source of all tissue macrophages. Many, such as those in the brain, liver and lung, were in fact laid down before birth and renew themselves; monocytes keep replacing macrophages in the gut and skin. This comes mostly from mouse fate-mapping; the human picture is less complete.
abundance: About 2-10% of circulating white blood cells in adult humans (roughly 0.2-0.8 × 10⁹ per litre of blood), most of them classical monocytes. Classical monocytes stay in the blood for about a day, non-classical ones for about a week.
